conditions.title: Choking (conscious adult or child)
steps: Ask the person 'Are you choking?' If they can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot cough, speak, or breathe, stand behind them and give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

If back blows do not clear the obstruction, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver): stand behind the person, place a fist above the navel, grasp it with your other hand, and pull sharply inward and upward.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive.
If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call emergency services immediately, and begin CPR.
warnings: Do not perform abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year old; use back blows and chest thrusts instead.
Do not perform abdominal thrusts on visibly pregnant or very obese individuals; use chest thrusts instead.
Call emergency services immediately if the obstruction does not clear.

source.reference: IFRC International First Aid Guidelines 2025 — Airway obstruction / choking chapter

conditions.title: Severe external bleeding
steps: Call emergency services if bleeding is severe or does not stop.
Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with a clean cloth or dressing.
If bleeding continues, add more dressings on top of the first without removing it, and increase pressure.
Elevate the injured limb above heart level if possible and if no fracture is suspected.
Once bleeding is controlled, secure the dressing firmly with a bandage without cutting off circulation.
If a limb wound continues to bleed severely despite direct pressure and a tourniquet is available and you are trained, apply it above the wound as a last resort.
warnings: Do not remove an embedded object from a wound; pad and bandage around it instead.
Watch for signs of shock (pale skin, rapid breathing, weakness) and treat accordingly.
Use gloves or a barrier if available to reduce infection risk.

source.reference: American Red Cross Responding to Emergencies — Bleeding control chapter

conditions.title: Thermal burns
steps: Remove the person from the source of the burn and stop the burning process.
Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 10-20 minutes.
Remove tight clothing and jewellery near the burn before swelling starts, unless stuck to the skin.
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, non-fluffy dressing or clean cling film.
Treat for shock if needed and monitor breathing.
Seek emergency medical care for burns larger than the person's palm, burns on the face/hands/genitals, or full-thickness (third-degree) burns.
warnings: Do not apply ice, butter, oil, or ointments to a burn.
Do not burst blisters.
Do not use adhesive dressings directly on a burn.

source.reference: St John Ambulance First Aid Reference Guide — Burns and scalds chapter

conditions.title: CPR (adult, unresponsive and not breathing normally)
steps: Check for danger, then check responsiveness by tapping the shoulders and shouting.
If unresponsive, call emergency services (or direct someone else to) and ask for an AED if available.
Open the airway with a head-tilt, chin-lift and check for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
If not breathing normally, begin chest compressions: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, at least 5 cm deep, at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute.
Give 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths if trained and willing; otherwise continue compression-only CPR.
Continue cycles of 30:2 until the person shows signs of life, an AED arrives, or emergency responders take over.
warnings: Do not delay starting compressions to check for a pulse.
Use an AED as soon as it is available and follow its voice prompts.
Compression-only CPR is an acceptable alternative if you are untrained or unwilling to give rescue breaths.

source.reference: WHO Basic Emergency Care 2018 — Basic life support / cardiac arrest chapter

conditions.title: Suspected bone fracture
steps: Keep the injured area still and support it in the position found; do not try to realign the bone.
If there is bleeding, control it with direct pressure around (not on top of) the deformity.
Immobilize the limb using a splint or padding, supporting the joints above and below the injury.
Check circulation, sensation, and movement beyond the injury (fingers or toes) before and after splinting.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling if available.
Arrange transport to emergency care; avoid moving the person unnecessarily.
warnings: Do not attempt to push a protruding bone back under the skin.
Do not give the person food or drink in case surgery is needed.
Seek immediate emergency care for an open fracture or loss of circulation beyond the injury.

source.reference: LRC Emergency Medical Responder 2021 — Musculoskeletal injuries chapter

conditions.title: Seizure / convulsion
steps: Stay with the person and time the seizure.
Clear the area of hard or sharp objects to prevent injury.
Place something soft under their head if possible.
Do not restrain the person or put anything in their mouth.
Once the seizure stops, place the person in the recovery position and check breathing.
Call emergency services if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, repeats without recovery, or this is the person's first known seizure.
warnings: Never put anything, including your fingers, in the person's mouth during a seizure.
Do not hold the person down.
Call emergency services immediately if the person is injured, has difficulty breathing afterward, or the seizure occurs in water.

source.reference: WHO Basic Emergency Care 2018 — Neurological emergencies chapter

conditions.title: Shock (circulatory collapse)
steps: Call emergency services.
Lay the person down and, if there is no suspected spinal or leg injury, raise their legs slightly.
Keep the person warm with a blanket or coat, but avoid overheating.
Treat any obvious cause, such as controlling severe bleeding.
Do not give the person anything to eat or drink.
Monitor breathing and level of responsiveness continuously until help arrives.
warnings: Signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid breathing, and confusion or weakness.
Do not raise the legs if a leg fracture, spinal injury, or head injury is suspected.
Shock can be life-threatening and worsens quickly; treat it as an emergency.

source.reference: LRC Emergency Medical Technician 2020 — Shock and perfusion chapter

conditions.title: Unconscious but breathing normally (recovery position)
steps: Check responsiveness and confirm the person is breathing normally.
Call emergency services.
Kneel beside the person and place the arm nearest you at a right angle to their body, palm up.
Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of their hand against the near cheek.
Grasp the far leg above the knee and pull it up, keeping the foot on the ground, then roll the person toward you onto their side.
Tilt the head back slightly to keep the airway open and monitor breathing continuously until help arrives.
warnings: Do not place someone in the recovery position if a spinal injury is suspected unless the airway is at risk; prioritize airway over spinal precautions in that case.
Recheck breathing regularly while waiting for emergency services.
If breathing stops at any point, begin CPR immediately.

source.reference: DLPA First Responder Training 2026 — Unconscious patient management chapter
